summary: FieldShift helps farmers explore crop rotations using NASA Earth observations, agricultural crop references, and their own priorities. Our prototype focuses on a study point in Kafr El Sheikh, Egypt, combining five years of NASA POWER weather data with quality-screened MODIS vegetation observations and a 15-crop catalog. It compares two-season crop sequences, explains their suitability, and flags water constraints instead of forcing unsuitable recommendations. The result is a transparent starting point for climate-aware planning—not a promise of higher yield or a replacement for local agricultural expertise.
details:
## FieldShift — Earth Data for Smarter Crop Rotations

### The problem we address

Choosing what to plant next involves balancing water availability, seasonal heat, crop diversity, and the farmer’s priorities. A rotation that appears attractive may require more water than is available, while repeating familiar crops can limit opportunities to introduce legumes or diversify the sequence.

FieldShift addresses the challenge of using NASA Earth observations and agricultural knowledge to make these trade-offs easier to understand. Our prototype focuses on a study point in Kafr El Sheikh, Egypt, rather than claiming to represent every farm in the governorate.

### What we built and its main use

We built a working, explainable crop-rotation decision-support engine. A user provides the previous crop and its season, water access, and priorities such as water conservation, soil-health considerations, and heat resilience.

The engine generates two-season crop sequences, checks their compatibility with declared water constraints, and returns up to three ranked alternatives with explanations, reference sources, and limitations. It can also display a supported current rotation as a comparison-only baseline.

A main use is helping a farmer or agricultural adviser explore alternatives before deciding what to plant next. If no option passes the water screen, the engine returns no recommendation and explains why, instead of forcing three unsuitable choices.

The delivered AI-only prototype runs directly in Python using a JSON input file and produces structured JSON results. An optional local FastAPI interface is also included. This demonstration does not depend on a completed mobile application.

### How the data supports the solution

Our Kafr El Sheikh study point is located at **31.11°N, 30.94°E**. Its historical dataset contains **1,826 daily NASA POWER records covering 2021–2025**, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, and solar radiation. These records provide historical climate context for comparing crop sequences and screening water and heat constraints. The evaporative-demand proxy used in scoring is not a measured irrigation requirement.

The dataset also contains **115 NASA MODIS vegetation composites**. Only observations passing the strict-good quality screen are used as vegetation context, and accepted observations remain on their actual composite dates. We do not manufacture daily satellite measurements or interpret NDVI as measured soil moisture.

A separate **15-crop agricultural reference catalog** supplies crop characteristics and water-reference ranges. These crop references are not NASA measurements. Egyptian Berseem clover is retained with a documented, treatment-specific water reference from Sakha research rather than being confused with alfalfa.

### How the engine works

TerraShift uses explicit rules and weighted suitability calculations, not a black-box prediction model. Users can change their priorities and understand why rankings change.

Water screening can exclude unsuitable options before ranking. Soil-health indicators reflect crop roles and a stated legume heuristic; they do not represent measured improvements in the farmer’s soil. Income scoring remains neutral because reliable local prices, costs, and yield outcomes are unavailable.

### Working features, evidence, and limitations

Working features include historical-data loading, crop-sequence generation, configurable priorities, water screening, ranked explanations, source metadata, and safe empty results.

Automated software tests and reference-based safety checks have been completed. Source checks also compared the weather records and a sample of vegetation observations with NASA responses. These checks support software reliability and source consistency—not a claim of agricultural accuracy.

The engine has not been trained on expert-ranked rotations or verified farm outcomes. A single study point is not a governorate average or a confirmed farm field. Recommendations still require local review, particularly for soil conditions, crop calendars, irrigation management, pests, and market factors.

### Tools, languages, hardware, and software

The tested AI engine uses **Python, NumPy, Pandas, Pydantic, and FastAPI**, with **Pytest and Ruff** supporting software checks. CSV and Excel store datasets and references; JSON carries inputs, configuration, and results. It runs on a standard computer without specialized sensors or a dedicated GPU.

Wider application development included **Flutter/Dart mobile work and .NET/C# backend work**. Integration of the corrected Python engine into that application is separate from the independently tested AI-only demonstration.

AI-assisted tools included ChatGPT Go for data discovery, Gemini for API/backend and chatbot work, Codex for AI implementation, Google Antigravity for Flutter development, and Manus for data corrections, checks, and documentation.

### Benefits and future plans

FieldShift aims to make climate-informed rotation comparisons more accessible and support clearer conversations between farmers and agricultural specialists. Its current benefit is transparent comparison, not a proven increase in yield or profit.

Next, we hope to collect expert-ranked cases and field outcomes, incorporate measured local soil information and crop calendars, and calibrate water and economic assumptions. We would then evaluate recommendations on held-out cases before claiming real-world agricultural performance.
